summary:
We developed Farmedia, an AI-powered smart agriculture platform designed to help farmers navigate drought, water stress, and sudden frost risks. To test the reliability of our model under real pressure, we anchored our baseline in the severe April 2020 climate crisis in Weld County, Colorado (40.2827° N, -104.6872° W). Farmedia brings six distinct NASA satellite datasets together under one roof—combining NASA POWER meteorological metrics, SMAP L3 soil moisture, OpenET daily water consumption, MODIS vegetation health indices, and NSIDC soil freeze-thaw records.
To keep farmers from getting overwhelmed by complex charts and raw numbers, we built SarpAI, a conversational assistant placed right at the bottom of the platform. Farmers can chat with SarpAI just like they would with a trusted agronomist—asking everyday questions like "What will the temperature be tomorrow?" or "What should I plant in my field right now?"—and receive clear, practical answers backed by satellite data. In short, Farmedia turns space-based intelligence into everyday field decisions, saving water, preventing crop losses from frost and drought, cutting operational costs, and paving the way for resilient farming worldwide.
details:
Farmedia: Project Overview & Technical Documentation

The climate crisis is placing unprecedented pressure on global agriculture. Due to unseasonal temperature drops, prolonged droughts, and erratic precipitation patterns, farmers are struggling more than ever to predict when to plant their crops, whether the soil carries a hidden frost risk, or how much water their fields actually require. Traditional farming calendars and local observations passed down through generations can no longer keep up with these rapid climate fluctuations. That is why we developed Farmedia—to transform complex Earth observation data and satellite telemetry from space into clear, reliable, and actionable daily decisions for farmers on the ground.

What It Does & How It Works (Multi-Layered Data Fusion)

When a farmer, agricultural cooperative, or agronomist selects a specific farmland area on the map or enters its geographic coordinates, Farmedia’s backend executes a multi-layered satellite and climate analysis for that exact location. Rather than relying on a single meteorological metric, our system performs multi-source data fusion—simultaneously integrating six distinct NASA and Earth observation datasets to provide a holistic view of field conditions from the atmosphere down to the root zone:

  1. SMAP L3 Radiometer Global Daily 9 km: Measures surface and root-zone soil moisture levels to scientifically determine actual drought severity and precise irrigation needs.
  2. OpenET Daily Evapotranspiration Exploration: Calculates the total daily water returned to the atmosphere from crops (transpiration) and soil (evaporation), establishing an accurate, field-level water budget.
  3. MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day: Uses high-resolution satellite imagery to monitor vegetation health, chlorophyll activity, and how crops biologically respond to drought or thermal stress from space.
  4. Probabilistic Freeze-Thaw Record: Detects sudden spring freeze-thaw cycles and risk probabilities in advance—especially during transitional periods when air temperatures appear warm—providing critical early warnings.
  5. NASA POWER Data Access Viewer: Tracks core atmospheric parameters—including ambient temperature, relative humidity, precipitation regimes, wind speed, and solar radiation—to map localized microclimate conditions.
  6. ECOSTRESS Tiled Land Surface Temperature: Measures high-resolution land surface temperature (LST) from the International Space Station (ISS), detecting thermal stress, crop water use dynamics, and sudden temperature fluctuations across fields with a precise 70-meter pixel resolution.

Operational Pipeline

  • Proactive 24/7 Automated Alert System: Beyond interactive Q&A, background scripts continuously monitor active fields. If a critical threshold is breached (such as sudden frost probability or severe moisture drop), the system instantly triggers multi-channel warnings via Email and Streamlit Dashboard Notifications, ensuring preventive action before damage occurs.

Real-World Crisis Validation: The Weld County Case Study

To ensure our system performs effectively during a real climate emergency rather than remaining a purely theoretical model, we stress-tested Farmedia against a historical extreme weather event. We anchored our baseline in the severe drought and sudden spring frost anomaly that struck Weld County, Colorado (40.2827° N, -104.6872° W) one of the most vital agricultural regions in the United States—in April 2020. In this validation study, Farmedia successfully detected critical soil moisture depletion and escalating water stress via SMAP and OpenET, while cross-validating freeze-thaw records with NASA POWER temperature data to flag early-planting hazards ahead of the sudden frost wave.

How Our Project Is Creative: The SarpAI Decision Engine

Even with the world’s most advanced satellite telemetry available, no farmer on the ground has the time or technical background to sit down and interpret complex climatological charts (netCDF/GeoTIFF files) or raw remote-sensing metrics. The most creative and transformative feature of Farmedia is SarpAI, our conversational AI assistant integrated directly into the platform to completely eliminate this technical barrier.

Just like consulting an experienced agronomist, farmers can ask SarpAI everyday questions in natural language, such as "Is there a frost risk in my field this week?" or "Does my soil need irrigation right now?" SarpAI does not act as a passive text generator; it instantly scans all six underlying satellite datasets for the user's selected coordinates, cross-validates the relationships between metrics, and delivers clear, cost-saving, and crop-protecting recommendations ready for immediate action.

Tools, Coding Languages & Development Workflow

We built Farmedia’s data ingestion, coordinate-based spatiotemporal alignment, statistical analysis, and backend architecture entirely in Python, leveraging modern data science libraries for data cleaning, model validation, and system integration. Throughout the development lifecycle, we actively utilized AI-assisted development tools for data analysis structuring, algorithm optimization, coding, and debugging, enabling rapid prototyping and high code reliability.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

As the SARP SYSTEMS team, we centered Farmedia’s architecture and user experience around four foundational engineering principles:

  1. Scientific Reliability & Cross-Validation: Eliminating single-source error margins by letting meteorology, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and freeze-thaw datasets cross-check one another.
  2. Low Cognitive Load (Simplicity First): Keeping the user interface intuitive and accessible, hiding complex satellite data behind natural language interaction.
  3. Zero Infrastructure Cost (Hardware Independence): Operating 100% via remote sensing with zero physical IoT sensors or on-site weather stations required, ensuring instant global scalability.
  4. Proactive Crisis Management: Prioritizing early-warning logic and automated alerts to take preventive action before crises strike.

Benefits & Intended Global Impact

The tangible benefits of Farmedia carry substantial economic and ecological value. By calculating actual soil moisture deficits and evapotranspiration rates, our system prevents over-irrigation—conserving rapidly depleting freshwater resources while lowering farmers' energy and water expenses. Simultaneously, by preventing premature planting ahead of hidden frost events, it eliminates wasted seed, fertilizer, and labor costs while minimizing climate-induced yield losses.

Because the NASA datasets we utilize provide global coverage, Farmedia can be seamlessly deployed anywhere in the world—from the arid plains of Anatolia to agricultural lands across Africa, South Asia, and Latin America—with zero infrastructure cost. With Farmedia, we aim to protect every drop of water and every seed planted through scientific data, leaving behind a sustainable food legacy for future generations.
